title: Chapter 158: Two Bowls of Water
html:
Chen Ge’s question drew three different reactions. The old man silently licked his fingers, savoring the memory of his last meal. The young woman’s eyes widened as she thrashed like a fish on dry land. Strangest of all, the middle-aged man alone kept his gaze fixed on Chen Ge.

“Why are these three imprisoned in an abandoned hospital?” He approached the old man first. Two plastic bowls sat inside his cage. Though aware of Chen Ge’s presence, the old man showed no fear, merely crouching in the center and sucking grease from his fingers.

“He’s the one moved from the first sick hall.” However closely Chen Ge studied him, nothing else seemed remarkable. “His hair is growing in unevenly. Someone shaved him recently, so this sample must be fresh.”

The sight reminded him of the hair nailed beneath the nurses’ station. One bundle contained white strands mixed with black and likely belonged to the old man.

“His hair is already this long after being shaved. He must have been trapped here for quite a while.” Chen Ge had identified samples from four people, yet only three prisoners sat before him. “One person is missing.”

His gaze passed over the young woman and stopped on the middle-aged man’s long, tangled hair. “It doesn’t look as if anyone shaved him.”

That made Chen Ge warier. Shaving appeared to be the captor’s peculiar ritual, perhaps a way of tormenting victims. Why spare this man? Did he know the captor—or was he the captor?

The thought disturbed him. In the passage between the first two sick halls, he had glimpsed an unfamiliar, asymmetrical face twisted out of shape.

Someone able to roam freely and follow him through the buildings was probably involved. Yet the middle-aged prisoner was suspicious as well. Perhaps more than one killer stalked the hospital, caging victims together.

Chen Ge tightened his grip on the mallet as an even darker possibility occurred to him. What if everyone in this hospital except me is a killer?

The possibility was remote. After thinking it through, he turned to the woman. Neither man seemed willing to answer, so he decided to remove her gag and seek information from her instead.

“Don’t worry. I’m here to rescue you.” He tested the lock. Without a key, breaking open all three cages with only a mallet would take an unknown amount of time.

The young woman seemed terrified of any living person. As soon as he approached, she moaned through the gag and shook her head and bound hands.

“Stay calm. I won’t hurt you.” Just as he reached for the gag, the middle-aged man finally spoke.

“I advise you to keep her gag on; she is very noisy.”

Chen Ge turned to a pair of dark, guarded eyes. Whether the man regarded everyone this way or only him was impossible to tell. Disgust seemed to radiate from the prisoner, as if everything Chen Ge did repelled him.

“Noisy?” Conversation did not frighten Chen Ge; silence did. As long as these people spoke, he had a chance to extract useful information.

“Yes, very noisy,” the middle-aged man answered succinctly. He seemed to think that communication was something disgusting as well.

“Why? Was she traumatized?” The middle-aged man ignored both questions.

Only when Chen Ge reached into the cage did he mutter, “Don’t know.”

“Then what do you know? If you don’t know her, do you know the old man?” Chen Ge asked what had been troubling him. “Why does his cage contain two plastic bowls while yours and hers contain only one?”

“I’ll tell you if you leave her gagged. She is extremely noisy.” The man’s fixation made Chen Ge curious, but he agreed—at least outwardly. “Fine, provided you don’t lie to me.”

“I never lie.” Seated in his cage, the man began in a gravelly voice. “The old man was frail and bad-tempered. After his wife left him, he depended entirely on his son. The son was a doctor. His salary was modest but enough to support them both. Then the old man took an interest in a widow and remarried. His son did not object; he moved out and continued sending money every month.

“Then misfortune struck. People said that treating psychiatric patients for too long drove the son, himself a psychiatrist, insane. He injured several patients, lost his job, and was sued by their families until he had nothing left.

“Treatment at a public psychiatric hospital cost four thousand yuan a month, money he did not have. With nowhere else to turn, he was admitted to the hospital where he had once worked, which charged far less than a public institution.

“The doctor became a patient. That reversal pushed him deeper into madness, and he remained untreated until the hospital closed.

“While the son was hospitalized, the old man’s health deteriorated. He was too old to work, and his entire government stipend went toward medical fees. Eventually, his second wife divorced him. When the hospital closed and his son returned home, the old man begged him to recover and rebuild his life.

“Soon afterward, the son reportedly bit someone in their village. His episodes made him violently destructive. With no other option, the old man built an iron cage and locked his son inside.

“That continued until the old man himself fell ill. He could barely feed himself, much less obtain treatment for either of them.

“Watching his son worsen inside the cage, he finally made a decision.

“He waited for his son’s next episode and set two bowls outside the bars. One held clean water; the other contained rat poison. He intended to let his son choose whether to live or die.”

The middle-aged man’s expression never changed, yet his face grew steadily paler, as though the story were draining him. “That is why the old man’s cage contains two bowls of water.”

The tale reminded Chen Ge of the message beneath the nurses’ station: I will repay everything you have done to me.
